Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The United States needs a new law requiring that the president consult with Congress before going to war, a blue-ribbon panel led by two former secretaries of state said Tuesday. James Baker, left, and Warren Christopher led a panel that recommended a new War Powers Act. The current War Powers Resolution is "ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced," James Baker said in a joint appearance with Warren Christopher, announcing the results of the study they led. The recommendation follows failed efforts by Democrats in Congress to put a stop to the war in Iraq or to put conditions on President Bush's conduct of it. Congress passed a joint resolution to authorize armed force against Iraq in 2002, but some Bush opponents say it should not have been interpreted as a blank check for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation. Baker, who served in George H.W. Bush's administration, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said their project was not prompted by any specific war, with Christopher adding that the commission had "tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here." "We didn't direct this report at any particular conflict," Baker added. The existing law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since it was passed as a response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher said. It requires presidents to report regularly to Congress about ongoing conflicts, but the provision has been flouted. "No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973," former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, said Tuesday. The panel, formally called the National War Powers Commission, said a new law should be created requiring the president to consult with key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than a week, or within three days of doing so in the case of operations that need to be kept secret. It should also make clear exactly who the president needed to consult. The panel suggests that the president talk to "a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees." The new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher said. Congress, in turn, would have to declare war or vote on a "resolution of approval" within 30 days, they said. If a resolution of approval failed, any member of Congress could introduce a "resolution of disapproval," but it was not clear that such an act would stop a war in progress. Christopher was unable to say in the news conference what practical effect congressional disapproval would have. Baker said the commission had been in touch with the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as leaders of Congress. He declined to reveal what they thought of the proposal, but said: "We haven't gotten a negative reaction." Congress has not officially declared war since 1942, when the United States entered formal hostilities with the Axis powers in World War II. But since then, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq. The Constitution makes the president the commander in chief of the armed forces, but gives Congress the power to declare war and approve military budgets. Baker and Christopher's group included both Republicans and Democrats and held seven meetings over 14 months.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The United States needs a new law requiring the president to consult Congress before going to war, a blue-ribbon panel led by former Secretaries of State James Baker and Warren Christopher said Tuesday.

Baker and Christopher led the panel that recommended replacing the current War Powers Resolution with a new War Powers Act.

The existing resolution is “ineffective, and it should be repealed and it should be replaced,” Baker said during a joint appearance with Christopher to announce the findings of their study.

The recommendation follows unsuccessful efforts by congressional Democrats to end the war in Iraq or impose conditions on President Bush’s conduct of it. Congress passed a joint resolution in 2002 authorizing the use of armed force against Iraq, but some Bush opponents argue that it should not have been interpreted as a blank check for the United States to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf nation.

Baker, who served in the administration of President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said their project was not prompted by any specific war. Christopher added that the commission had “tried very hard not to call balls and strikes on past history here.”

“We didn’t direct this report at any particular conflict,” Baker added.

The existing law, the War Powers Resolution of 1973, has been regarded as unconstitutional by every president since it was enacted in response to the Vietnam War, Baker and Christopher said. It requires presidents to report regularly to Congress on ongoing conflicts, but that provision has been disregarded.

“No president has ever made a submission to Congress pursuant to the War Powers Resolution since 1973,” former Sen. Slade Gorton, a Republican member of the committee, said Tuesday.

The panel, formally known as the National War Powers Commission, recommended creating a new law requiring the president to consult key members of Congress before sending troops into combat expected to last more than a week—or, in the case of operations that must remain secret, within three days of doing so.

The law should also clearly specify whom the president must consult. The panel suggested that the president confer with “a joint Congressional committee made up of the leaders of the House and the Senate as well as the chairmen and ranking members of key committees.”

The new committee would have a permanent professional staff with access to intelligence information, Baker and Christopher said.

Congress, in turn, would be required to declare war or vote on a “resolution of approval” within 30 days, they said. If the resolution of approval failed, any member of Congress could introduce a “resolution of disapproval,” although it was unclear whether such a measure would halt a war already in progress.

At the news conference, Christopher was unable to explain what practical effect congressional disapproval would have.

Baker said the commission had contacted the presidential campaigns of Democrat Barack Obama and Republican John McCain, as well as congressional leaders. He declined to disclose their views on the proposal but said, “We haven’t gotten a negative reaction.”

Congress has not formally declared war since 1942, when the United States entered formal hostilities against the Axis powers in World War II. Since then, however, presidents have sent troops into countries including Korea, Vietnam, Grenada, and Iraq.

The Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the armed forces while granting Congress the authority to declare war and approve military budgets.

Baker and Christopher’s bipartisan group included both Republicans and Democrats and convened seven times over 14 months.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — A bipartisan commission headed by former secretaries of state James Baker and Warren Christopher recommended Tuesday that the United States replace its current war-powers law with legislation requiring presidents to confer with Congress before initiating military action.

Baker said the existing War Powers Resolution does not work and should be abolished in favor of a new statute. He and Christopher announced the findings of the panel, formally known as the National War Powers Commission, during a joint appearance.

The proposal comes after congressional Democrats unsuccessfully attempted either to end the Iraq war or impose restrictions on President George W. Bush’s management of it. In 2002, Congress approved a joint resolution permitting the use of military force against Iraq. Some Bush critics, however, argue that the measure was never intended to give the administration unlimited authority to invade and occupy the Persian Gulf country.

Baker, who served in the administration of President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who was secretary of state under President Bill Clinton, emphasized that their review was not a response to any one military conflict. Christopher said the commission had deliberately avoided judging earlier episodes, while Baker reiterated that the report was not aimed at a particular war.

According to Baker and Christopher, every president since the War Powers Resolution became law in 1973 has considered it unconstitutional. Enacted in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, the resolution directs presidents to provide Congress with regular reports on continuing military operations, but that requirement has routinely been disregarded.

Former Republican Sen. Slade Gorton, a member of the commission, said Tuesday that no president since 1973 had ever formally submitted a report to Congress under the resolution.

The commission proposed a replacement law that would compel the president to consult designated congressional leaders before deploying U.S. forces into combat likely to continue for longer than seven days. If secrecy were essential, those consultations could instead occur within three days after the operation began.

The legislation would also specify which lawmakers must be included. The panel recommended creating a joint House-Senate committee composed of congressional leaders and the chairmen and ranking minority members of important committees. Baker and Christopher said this body would be supported by a permanent professional staff authorized to receive intelligence.

Under the plan, Congress would then have 30 days either to issue a formal declaration of war or approve the operation through a separate resolution. If the approval measure did not pass, any lawmaker could offer a resolution opposing the military action. It remained uncertain, however, whether passage of such a disapproval resolution would bring an ongoing conflict to an end. At the news conference, Christopher could not explain what concrete consequences congressional rejection would produce.

Baker said the commission had communicated with the presidential campaigns of Democratic nominee Barack Obama and Republican nominee John McCain, along with congressional leaders. Although he would not disclose their specific views, he said none had responded negatively.

The last formal declaration of war by Congress occurred in 1942, when the United States entered official hostilities against the Axis powers during World War II. Nevertheless, presidents have since deployed American forces to such countries as Korea, Vietnam, Grenada and Iraq.

The Constitution designates the president as commander in chief of the military, while assigning Congress the authority to declare war and authorize defense spending.

Made up of both Democrats and Republicans, the Baker-Christopher commission met seven times during a 14-month period.

The commission argued that the existing law had failed to establish a workable process for cooperation between the executive and legislative branches.

Under the proposed legislation, the president would be required to consult key members of Congress before initiating combat operations expected to last longer than one week. The goal was to ensure that congressional leaders received timely information and had a meaningful opportunity to discuss significant military commitments, while preserving the president’s ability to respond quickly to emergencies.

The commission noted that every president since the resolution’s enactment had regarded at least some of its provisions as unconstitutional. In practice, presidents had also routinely avoided or disregarded its reporting requirements, weakening the law’s ability to constrain executive action or promote effective consultation with Congress.

The recommendation came after congressional Democrats had unsuccessfully attempted to end the Iraq War or attach conditions to its continuation. Nevertheless, the commission maintained that its proposal was not directed at Iraq or any other specific conflict. Instead, it presented the plan as a long-term institutional reform intended to clarify the respective responsibilities of Congress and the president.

The debate was nevertheless shaped by controversy over the Iraq War. Critics argued that Congress’s 2002 authorization for the use of military force should not have been interpreted as unrestricted approval for the invasion and prolonged occupation of Iraq. In their view, the experience demonstrated the need for clearer authorization, stronger consultation requirements, and more sustained congressional involvement once military operations were underway.

counterfactuals.output:
# Bipartisan commission urges overhaul of presidential war powers

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** A bipartisan commission led by two former secretaries of state has proposed replacing the 1973 War Powers Resolution with a law requiring the president to consult Congress before committing U.S. forces to significant armed conflict.

The National War Powers Commission, co-chaired by former Secretary of State James Baker, a Republican, and former Secretary of State Warren Christopher, a Democrat, said the existing law has failed to create a workable process for cooperation between the executive and legislative branches.

Its proposed War Powers Consultation Act would require the president to confer with a permanent congressional committee before ordering troops into major hostilities. When advance consultation is not possible because of an emergency, the president would have to meet with lawmakers shortly after military action begins.

The requirement would generally apply to combat operations expected to last more than a week, while excluding routine training, intelligence activities, disaster relief and some limited operations.

Under the proposal, Congress would be required to vote within 30 days on whether to approve a military campaign that had not already been authorized. If lawmakers rejected or failed to approve the action, members could pursue an expedited resolution of disapproval.

Unlike the War Powers Resolution, the commission’s plan would not automatically require the withdrawal of U.S. forces after a set period. The 1973 measure directs presidents to end unauthorized deployments after 60 days, with an additional 30 days allowed for withdrawal, but successive administrations have disputed its constitutionality and often avoided formally acknowledging that the deadline applies.

The commission said decades of conflict over the law have left both branches without clear procedures for making decisions that can put American troops at risk.

Supporters of the proposal argue that mandatory consultation and prompt congressional votes would make elected officials more accountable. Critics may contend that replacing the withdrawal deadline could weaken Congress’ ability to stop a president from continuing military operations.

The plan would still need congressional approval and the president’s signature to become law.

## Bipartisan panel condemns War Powers Resolution as ineffective, urges new consultation law

**WASHINGTON, July 8, 2008** — A bipartisan commission led by former Secretaries of State James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher has concluded that the 1973 War Powers Resolution has failed to regulate the use of American military force and should be replaced with a law requiring sustained consultation between the president and Congress.

The **National War Powers Commission**, assembled through the University of Virginia’s Miller Center of Public Affairs, said the existing resolution is “impractical and ineffective” and has done little to resolve the constitutional struggle between the executive and legislative branches over decisions to send U.S. forces into hostilities.

Baker, who served under President George H.W. Bush, and Christopher, who served under President Bill Clinton, said both branches have contributed to the law’s failure. Presidents of both parties have generally refused to accept that the resolution can constitutionally restrict their authority as commander in chief, while Congress has often avoided clear votes on military operations.

“The rule of law is undermined when the nation’s leaders are unable or unwilling to agree on a workable process for making one of the most consequential decisions government faces,” the commission said in its report.

### Proposed replacement

The panel recommended repealing the War Powers Resolution and replacing it with a **War Powers Consultation Act**, intended to encourage consultation before the United States enters a “significant armed conflict.”

Under the proposal, the president would be required to consult senior congressional leaders before committing U.S. forces to major hostilities. When emergencies or the need for secrecy made advance consultation impossible, the president would have to confer with lawmakers within three calendar days.

The commission defined a significant armed conflict generally as combat operations lasting, or expected to last, more than one week. Certain activities—including routine training, covert operations, humanitarian missions and disaster relief—would generally fall outside that definition unless they developed into sustained hostilities.

The measure would also create a permanent **Joint Congressional Consultation Committee** composed of top House and Senate leaders and senior members of the committees responsible for foreign affairs, armed services and intelligence. The committee would meet regularly with the president and senior national-security officials and would receive the information needed to assess contemplated or continuing military action.

Once troops entered a significant conflict, the president would submit a report explaining the circumstances, objectives and legal basis for the deployment. Congress would then be expected to vote within 30 days on whether to approve the operation. If it failed to pass an authorization, lawmakers would have access to an expedited procedure for considering a resolution of disapproval.

Unlike the 1973 resolution, however, the proposed law would not automatically require the withdrawal of troops after a fixed period.

### Rejection of the 60-day deadline

The existing War Powers Resolution was enacted over President Richard Nixon’s veto during the final years of the Vietnam War. It requires presidents to notify Congress within 48 hours after introducing U.S. forces into hostilities and generally directs that those forces be withdrawn within 60 days unless Congress authorizes the operation or extends the deadline. A further 30 days may be allowed for a safe withdrawal.

Successive presidents have questioned the constitutionality of those provisions. Administrations have often filed reports “consistent with” the resolution without conceding that it legally binds the president.

The commission said the automatic withdrawal mechanism had not worked as intended and could produce damaging uncertainty during a military operation. It also found that the resolution encouraged technical arguments over whether troops had entered “hostilities,” rather than meaningful discussion about strategy, objectives and costs.

The panel did not attempt to settle the longstanding constitutional dispute over whether the president or Congress has the final authority to initiate particular uses of force. Instead, it sought to establish a political process under which both branches would have to state and defend their positions.

### No automatic answer to constitutional dispute

The Constitution gives Congress the power to declare war, raise and fund armed forces, and regulate the military. It designates the president as commander in chief. The boundaries between those powers have been contested throughout American history, particularly as presidents have undertaken limited wars, air campaigns and other military actions without formal declarations of war.

The commission said its proposal was deliberately designed to avoid relying on the courts. Judges have generally been reluctant to decide war-powers disputes, often treating them as political questions or finding that lawmakers lack standing to sue.

Instead, the proposed act would place responsibility directly on elected officials. Presidents would have a formal obligation to consult and explain. Members of Congress would be pressed to vote for or against a military commitment rather than relying on silence, ambiguous funding measures or later criticism.

### Bipartisan membership and political timing

The commission included former legislators, cabinet officials, judges and diplomats from both major parties. Its members included former Secretary of State George Shultz, former Defense Secretary William Perry, former Attorney General Edwin Meese III, former White House counsel Lloyd Cutler, former Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle and former lawmakers Lee Hamilton and Slade Gorton, among others.

Its report arrived as the United States remained deeply engaged in Iraq and Afghanistan and as the 2008 presidential election focused heavily on national security. The panel urged Congress and the next administration to take up the proposed law in 2009.

Baker and Christopher emphasized that the commission was not seeking to strengthen one branch at the expense of the other. Baker said presidents need enough flexibility to respond quickly to threats, while Christopher stressed that Congress cannot be excluded from decisions that may place American service members in prolonged combat.

The proposal’s central premise is that no statute can eliminate disagreement over war powers, but the law can require earlier communication, better information and public accountability.

Whether Congress would accept that framework remained uncertain. Some lawmakers were likely to object that eliminating the 60-day withdrawal requirement would surrender congressional authority. Advocates of broad presidential power, meanwhile, could resist any mandatory consultation regime as an intrusion on the commander in chief.

The commission acknowledged those disagreements but argued that the existing system was worse: a law routinely disputed by presidents, inconsistently invoked by Congress and unable to produce a dependable process for deciding when and how the nation goes to war.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the Baker-Christopher commission proposed changing the balance of war-making authority between the president and Congress, with context about Iraq, Vietnam, and past U.S. conflicts.
counterfactuals.output:
The **Baker–Christopher Commission**, formally the bipartisan **National War Powers Commission**, proposed replacing the largely ineffective **War Powers Resolution of 1973** with a system built around mandatory consultation and prompt congressional voting.

### Historical context

The Constitution divides war powers: Congress declares war, raises and funds the armed forces, while the president is commander in chief. That division became increasingly unsettled as presidents used force without formal declarations of war.

- In **Korea**, President Truman committed forces under a U.N. mandate without a congressional declaration.
- During **Vietnam**, Congress passed the broad Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, but presidents expanded the war far beyond what many legislators believed they had approved. Congress responded by enacting the **War Powers Resolution** over President Nixon’s veto.
- That resolution required notification within 48 hours and generally called for troops to be withdrawn after 60 days—plus a 30-day withdrawal period—unless Congress authorized the operation. Presidents of both parties questioned its constitutionality, often avoided triggering it, and Congress seldom enforced its deadlines.
- Later operations in places such as **Lebanon, Somalia, Kosovo, and Iraq** exposed the same uncertainty. Congress expressly authorized the 2003 Iraq invasion through the **2002 Iraq AUMF**, but disputes over the war’s expansion, duration, and management demonstrated that one-time authorization did not ensure sustained consultation or accountability.

The commission was created amid the Iraq War and issued its report in 2008. It was chaired by former secretaries of state **James Baker** and **Warren Christopher**.

### The proposed change

The commission recommended a new **War Powers Consultation Act** with three main features:

1. **A permanent congressional consultation body**  
   Senior House and Senate leaders and the chairs and ranking members of relevant committees would form a standing consultation committee. The president would have to consult it before beginning a “significant armed conflict,” except when emergencies made advance consultation impossible.

2. **Early presidential reporting**  
   If prior consultation was impossible, the president would have to consult Congress shortly afterward—generally within three days—and explain the conflict’s objectives, scope, legal basis, and expected duration.

3. **A required congressional vote**  
   Congress would have to consider the conflict within roughly 30 days. It could enact a declaration of war or specific authorization. If it did not approve, procedures would facilitate a vote expressing disapproval, forcing legislators to take a public position rather than avoiding responsibility.

### How this would shift the balance

The proposal was a compromise rather than a simple transfer of power to Congress.

- It would **strengthen Congress politically and institutionally** by guaranteeing early access to information, regular consultation, and a recorded vote.
- It would make it harder for presidents to confront Congress with a fully developed war as a fait accompli.
- But it would also **give presidents more operational flexibility** than the 1973 resolution appeared to allow. The commission would eliminate the automatic 60-day withdrawal mechanism and did not require advance congressional authorization in every case.
- A congressional resolution of disapproval would carry substantial political weight, but because a concurrent resolution cannot legally bind the president, Congress would still need binding legislation—potentially overcoming a veto—or use its appropriations power to compel withdrawal.

Thus, Baker and Christopher sought to replace an ostensibly restrictive but routinely evaded law with a more realistic bargain: **the president could respond quickly and command military operations, but Congress could no longer remain passive or ambiguous about a prolonged major conflict**. The proposal aimed to restore shared responsibility for war rather than give exclusive control to either branch.

**WASHINGTON —** A bipartisan blue-ribbon commission has recommended that presidents consult senior congressional leaders before sending U.S. troops into combat expected to last more than one week.

The National War Powers Commission said the proposed requirement would encourage cooperation between the executive and legislative branches while preserving the president’s ability to respond quickly to emergencies.

Under the commission’s plan, the president would confer with a permanent group of congressional leaders before beginning a “significant armed conflict,” defined generally as combat operations expected to continue for more than seven days. The group would include party leaders and senior members of committees responsible for national security and foreign policy.

If an urgent threat made advance consultation impractical, the president would be required to meet with lawmakers shortly after military operations began.

The bipartisan panel, led by former secretaries of state James A. Baker III and Warren Christopher, also called for replacing the 1973 War Powers Resolution. That law requires presidents to notify Congress after deploying forces and generally directs them to end unauthorized military action within 60 to 90 days. Successive administrations from both parties have questioned its constitutionality or resisted its restrictions.

The commission concluded that the existing law has failed to produce meaningful consultation between presidents and Congress. Its proposed framework would establish regular procedures for sharing information and debating major military commitments without attempting to resolve the long-running constitutional dispute over which branch has ultimate authority to initiate hostilities.

The recommendation would not require consultation for short-term operations, routine deployments, covert actions or immediate responses to attacks. Congress would have to enact legislation for the proposal to become binding.
